problems: Battles 1-10 all feel the same: one procedurally recoloured blob monster with a bigger HP bar and a turn counter. Battle 10 is a 'BOSS' that is just the same blob with horns and 119 HP, with no new attack pattern, arena or set piece. Abilities (stone, poison, rage...) come from a random roll, so they are not introduced on purpose. There are only 3 backgrounds across 30 battles.

Each swap waits for the whole cascade, the orb flight, the damage numbers and the monster's turn before you can move again (about 1.5-2s of dead time per move). On the phone my touch bot only got 8 swipes into a 40-poll window. The rhythm is wait-swipe-wait, not a fast combo rush. The cascade combos need a much bigger payoff (pitch-rising chain sound, slow-mo, screen-filling hit).

The VICTORY screen only shows stars, +gold and +XP. There is no tease of the next monster or region and no count-up. The phone map has the shared gb.js settings tab sitting on top of the HERO button. Upgrades/relics are plain DOM lists, and nothing surprising happens during a fight (no monster reactions, critters or golden runes).
rune-match.notes: Puzzle Quest-style match-3: swipe runes on an 8x8 board, and each colour becomes a sword, fire, ice, heal or shield spell against one monster per wave. It works on touch and mouse and the art is clean, but it is a slow, samey turn loop with 30 numbered battles.

problems: It is far too hard for kids from level 1. A bot typing at a steady 30 WPM with 97% accuracy got TRACED on server 1-1. At 40 WPM it barely passed 1-1 (trace 94%) and failed 1-2 and 1-3. At 50-55 WPM it still failed 1-2 and 1-3. Most 9-year-olds type at 15-25 WPM, so a typical kid never wins once. That breaks Rule 1 (an instant first win) completely.

The 'controls' are typing dense shell/regex/C++ lines full of symbols, e.g. kill -9 $(pgrep -f "watchdog") and later awk -F: '$3 >= 1000 && $7 !~ /nologin/'. On a phone that means the soft keyboard with symbol layers. This is the opposite of one or two buttons, and a typo can't be fixed with backspace, it just adds trace.

It is a green-on-black Matrix rain terminal with text in boxes: the 'AI look' and a wall of text by design. Every level is the same action (type lines, fill a bar) with a different list of lines. Feedback on each correct key is minimal, and there are no characters, no surprises and no set pieces. The phone tutorial caption runs off the screen ('Stay under 10...').
terminal-rush.notes: REMAKE PENDING: a remake scored 7 (needs 8) and was NOT shipped; it is saved on branch wip-tuneup-2026-11-19. Next week: finish it from that branch with these fixes: Add a second verb to the run: some gates are a jump gap or a slide pipe, where the word you type picks the move ('jump' / 'duck'), plus at least one route-split level per world where typing word A or word B picks the path.; Keep symbols and code out of the main 30 levels for kids (letters, capitals and simple ! ? only), and move the code lines into an optional 'Hacker' bonus world or Endless.; Clamp the next gate's word sign inside the screen (both 1280 px and 390 px) so the whole word and its combo tag are visible before you type.; Update build/meta.json to title 'Hacker Dash' with a kid-friendly blurb.. Original: A typing-speed game: type real-looking shell/code lines exactly to 'hack' 25 servers before a trace bar fills, with credits for upgrades. It is technically solid, but punishingly hard for kids and almost all reading.

problems: It is a calm Islanders-style score puzzle: pick a building card, click a hex, and get +1..+6. Many placements show '+0' with a small dust puff, and there is no chain reaction, no bigger combo fanfare and no moment that makes you grin. Every run is the same loop on the same island until you grind crowns (+23-27 per ~3-minute run) to buy the next island.

Phone controls are fiddly. The hexes are about 25px across at 390x700, and placing needs a double-tap on the exact tiny hex (tap to preview, tap again to place). The building cards cover the bottom of the island. This breaks Rule 3 (big hit areas, no tiny targets).

The world is static: buildings never animate (apart from windmill blades), and there are no villagers, boats, critters or weather events reacting to what you build. The UI uses emoji as art (gift, box, crown, dice in the HUD and upgrades). Runs end with a plain score card; 'New pack!' choices are the only decision, and there are no level goals or new twists per run.
tile-kingdom.notes: REMAKE PENDING: a remake scored 7 (needs 8) and was NOT shipped; it is saved on branch wip-tuneup-2026-11-19. Next week: finish it from that branch with these fixes: Make losing possible. Use tighter bags and goals that a greedy bot fails on bosses and from level 10 on, and add junk pieces or rock drops that fill the board so space runs out.; Make boss telegraphs punish you: if you ignore the Kraken's marked hex, it destroys a building and adds rocks. That way reading the '!' is what wins the fight.; Add a per-level twist that matters every turn (a rising tide that sinks one edge hex every 3 turns, goats that eat a hut if left untrapped), so 'one more move' feels tense.; Rename to Island Town in meta.json.. Original: A hex island city-scorer: place buildings from small packs, score points from neighbour adjacency, and pass score thresholds to earn more packs until you run out. Pretty low-poly art, but a slow, quiet number puzzle with little feedback.

problems: It is far too easy and shallow early on. A dumb greedy bot (hit the weakest enemy in reach, otherwise walk toward the nearest one) won battles 1-4 in 3-4 turns each, mostly with 2-3 stars, even though it lost a unit. Battles 1-4 are the same flat grass field with goblins, and only small terrain tweaks (river, forest, hills) separate them. Nothing in the first ~10 minutes needs real tactics.

Each unit action takes 4 taps: tap unit, tap tile, tap enemy to see a forecast, tap again to confirm (or tap self to wait), plus END each turn. That is a lot of fiddly tapping for Rule 3. On the phone the board rotates, and the shared gb.js gear tab covers the par/hourglass HUD.

There is little juice and no surprise. A hit is a small bump with -7 and a few pixels, with no hit-stop, crit slow-mo or KO fanfare. The level map is a plain grid of 20 grey boxes, the camp is a menu, and the victory screen has no tease of the next battle. There are no story beats, wandering critters or secret chests on maps.
tiny-tactics.notes: REMAKE PENDING: a remake scored 7 (needs 8) and was NOT shipped; it is saved on branch wip-tuneup-2026-11-19. Next week: finish it from that branch with these fixes: Fix the phone leaderboard: open GBBoard on 'click' (or setTimeout 350ms like Tiny Farm and Busy Bees) instead of on pointerdown.; Zoom the board to fill the screen height on desktop (tiles of about 80-90px) so hits and units read big.; Speed up the loop: auto-fast-forward enemy turns by default, and make early battles shorter and punchier (a 2-turn 'bonk the goblin raid' opener, a chest grab).; Make battles 3-4 losable for a bot that just charges in (archers on hills, a wolf pack that flanks).. Original: A small Fire Emblem-style grid tactics game: deploy knight, archer, mage and healer and fight goblins, orcs and wolves over 20 battles, with XP, levels and 3-star goals. The pixel sprites are nice, but the early battles are trivially easy and the inputs are tap-heavy.

problems: Levels 1-1 to 1-4 are the same idea with more trains (5 to 8) and 1-3 switches. My switch-only bot 3-starred all four with big time margins (34/42s, 36/45s, 44/53s, 43/54s) and never needed to brake. The first world needs a twist sooner: introduce braking, a fast express or a paint shed by level 3. The interesting mechanics (river bridges, road crossings, deserts, night) only arrive in world 2+.

The difficulty spike is sharp once the hazards arrive. In 2-5 (bridge + river, 7 switches, 10 trains) and 4-4 (road crossing) the switch-only bot crashed within 7-21s. Tap-the-train braking is never pressed in levels 1-4, so players reach the hard levels without practice. The crash screen is fine, but there is no 'so close!' or replay of what went wrong.

Delivering a train correctly needs a bigger payoff: a bigger chime and confetti burst at the station, a chain multiplier for back-to-back deliveries, and a slow-mo save when two trains just miss each other. Right now success is a small pop and a counter tick. The tutorial is long (about 30s across 6 steps) before the real first level.
junction-jam.notes: Tap switches (or press 1-9) to steer colour-coded toy trains from tunnels to matching stations without crashing, over 60 levels across themed worlds with bridges, road crossings, rivers and night, plus a Rush Hour mode, shop and diorama. A polished, readable, charming diorama look; the best of this batch, held back by a samey first world and modest reward juice.

problems: You aim blind. While you place a well, nothing shows where the marble will go (just a short arrow at the cannon). You press GO, the shot ends in about 1 second, then you guess again. It plays as trial and error, not skill, and the hint button is often the fastest way through.

Winning feels flat. The result is a bare 'GULP!' panel with 3 stars and 3 icon buttons: no count-up, no tease of the next level, no slow-mo as the marble falls in, and the black hole doesn't react. The marble is a plain glowing dot with no character.

Variety is thin and there are no surprises. World 1 (10 levels) is only walls plus 1-2 wells, and there are only 40 levels in total. No critters, golden events or secrets. Bug: if you press GO without re-dragging, the tutorial caption 'Drag it again to fine-tune' stays stuck over the results screen.
gravity-gulp.notes: Physics puzzle: drag attract/repel gravity wells onto the board, press GO, and the cannon's marble curves through stars into a black hole. Four worlds add moving walls, portals plus spikes, and multi-cannon levels. The phone layout rotates well.

problems: build/meta.json still lists 'Hex 2048' / 'Slide hexagon tiles six ways'. The title screen says 'Bee Merge', so the site card describes a different game (Rule 12).
Level 1 is still won in one tap, which is fine as an instant win, but levels 2-4 follow in 5-13 s each, so the first minute passes in a blur of results panels.
On desktop, bosses throw rocks onto the board, but it's easy to miss because the boss sits small in the left panel.
hex-merge.notes: Remade 2026-11-19 (was 2). Tap a honeycomb cell to drop the next honey tile, and 3 or more equal tiles merge and can chain. The fixes landed. It's harder now: the greedy bot lost levels 9 and 21, and a bot playing a random cell 40% of the time lost the bosses at levels 30, 40, 50 and 60 (it still beat level 20). There are 'N moves short of 3 stars' notes, and almost every results screen teases a NEW thing (golden honey, chain-3 HONEY FLOOD, grubs, spreading ice, hornet nests, thief, gusts). Bosses now throw rocks onto the board. It's charming and has one-tap controls. Ships once the meta title and blurb are updated.

problems: The hedges are solid walls with no hint of the way around. A straight-line flier, which is how a kid flies, gets stuck against them. My simple bot dropped from 3 stars to 1 star on days 1-3 and failed the Wasp Queen on day 5, partly from hedge snags plus the spoil timer.
The meadow art is still mostly flat grass with flowers. The bigger scrolling world doesn't have landmarks that make far zones feel like different places.
The spoil countdown number sits right on the bee trail and can be lost among the bees when the trail is long.
hive-mind.notes: Remade 2026-11-19 (was 3). Grab-and-race-home bee-train game. The fixes landed: a scrolling world up to about 1.9x the screen, hedges, a hive pointer with distance, a per-load 'nectar spoils' timer with ticking that speeds up, SPOILED / SO CLOSE feedback, and harder early stars. The phone 🏆 is fixed (opens and stays open). DASH no longer blocks play.

problems: Most puzzles are tiny and solved by just trying directions. BFS optimal solutions: levels 1-4 take 2-4 moves, and levels 11/21/31/41/51 take 4/5/5/6/5. Only level 60 takes 15. Par always equals the optimum, there are no hard spike levels, and 60 levels go by very fast.

The slide feels flat. The penguin glides with a few white specks: no squash or stretch on the bump, no ice-spray trail, no wobble or splash. Reaching a nest is a small chime and the win is a plain white modal (no count-up, no tease of the next level).

No surprises at all: no fish, seals, secrets, idle antics or golden nests. Bug: the tutorial's last step 'Oops? Tap undo' stays over the board and the win modal on later levels until you actually press undo.
ice-slide.notes: Grid ice-sliding puzzle: swipe or arrow keys slide the penguin until it bumps something. Chapters add pushable blocks, holes to fill, heat tiles that melt ice cubes, switches and gates, and several penguins moving at once. Controls are excellent and the art is cute and clean.

problems: Far too hard for a kid. A bot typing about 42 WPM at 95% accuracy LOSES level 1-4. The level 1-6 boss already needs quotes, colons and capitals (e.g. 'HAILSTORM.", citizens: the Storm), and later sectors are numbers, phrases and code. A typical 9-year-old types 15-25 WPM.
It's a reading and typing drill (symbols, code) for adults, not a game: the whole screen is text to read (Rule 9). 3 stars needs 96% accuracy plus 48 WPM.

Touch alone isn't enough: on the phone you need the OS keyboard, and falling words overlap the HUD (e.g. 'Havoc' over the WPM readout). The boss-clear results screen has no Next button (only home/retry/shop), and the meteors are plain rocks.
keystorm.notes: REMAKE PENDING: a remake scored 6 (needs 8) and was NOT shipped; it is saved on branch wip-tuneup-2026-11-19. Next week: finish it from that branch with these fixes: From 1-2 on, keep 2-4 short-word meteors falling at once with staggered heights, so a 20 WPM bot loses about 1 house per level and only gets 'Perfect defense' with good typing. Add slow-mo and 'SO CLOSE!' when a meteor is stopped just above a roof.; Use letters only (plus capitals) until world 3, and move symbols and code to an optional bonus world.; Fill the sky: clouds the meteors pass behind, birds and planes to avoid, a big boss shadow that grows, and parallax.; Update build/meta.json title and blurb to 'Meteor Typer'.. Original: Typing defence: words, numbers, phrases and code snippets fall on meteors. Type them to laser them before they hit the city, with combo multipliers, a nova bomb on Enter, a boss every 6 levels and a gem shop. Juicy explosions, but it's punishing and text-heavy.

problems: Every song plays exactly the same: tap and hold notes on 4 lanes over the same synthwave sun-and-grid backdrop, with only the lane colors and BPM changing. 15 songs bring no new note type, twist, boss song or scene change, so minute 20 feels like minute 2.

Songs run about 100 s and the first song on Easy is sparse (158 notes, roughly 1.5 per second). My first run scored an A at 93.7% with almost no challenge. Each S on Easy is worth 4 stars, so a decent player can unlock most of the list quickly, and on Hard the only difficulty is more notes.

The results screen has only Menu and Retry, with no Next button and no tease of the next song (only a small unlock line). Feedback is generic: a PERFECT pop, a few lane particles and a combo number. There's no hit-stop, no combo milestone fanfare and no reacting crowd or character, so nothing surprising ever happens.
beat-tapper.notes: A 4-lane falling-note rhythm game (DFJK or tap lanes) with procedurally synthesized songs, 3 difficulties, hold notes and S-to-D grades. It's tight and responsive, but you're tapping coloured pills down the same neon highway in every song.

problems: It's far too easy and short. My simple greedy bot (bake, merge the lowest pair, tap to serve) got 3 stars on levels 1-13 without losing a heart. Levels 2-6 lasted 7-27 seconds, and the 6x6 board is never more than a third full, so you're never under pressure.

Levels only change numbers: more customers, a second or third seat, higher tiers, one more flavor. Nothing new mechanically shows up level to level, and level 7 hard-gates you into a text-list shop (Speed, Heat, Patience, Tips, Auto oven) before you can continue.

Merges are weak: a small particle puff and a pop, with screen shake only from tier 6 up. The results card ('Sold out!', stars, +coins, Map/Next) has no count-up and no preview of the next level or customer. Customers are cute static animal heads with almost no reaction.
block-bakery.notes: A merge-and-serve puzzle: tap the oven (or Space) to bake cookies onto a 6x6 grid, drag identical pastries together to tier them up, and tap an item to serve animal customers whose patience bars run down. It looks clean and cute, but it's slow and pressure-free.

problems: The first casts are tiny. The starting line is only 60 m (about 180 px), so the whole dive and reel-up of your first several casts happens on the surface screen in about 3 seconds, and the tutorial's first cast often comes back 'No bite... +0'. The big 'drop deep into the abyss' feeling is gated behind 5+ line upgrades.

Early progress is a slow grind with no burst. My bot earned 6-50 coins per cast against upgrade costs of 20-140, and after 16 casts (about 4 minutes) it had only reached 360 m in the first water. New waters cost 1,200 / 9,000 / 45,000 coins, so a kid sees the same Sunny Shoals fish for a long time.

Catching a fish on the way up is just touching it with the hook: a small +coin float and white sparkle, and small fish are about 20 px at 1280 wide. Jelly stings and the reel-tension minigame (big fish only) are the only drama, the 'MAX DEPTH' toast covers the boat, and there's little juice on landing besides fish flying into the boat.
deep-cast.notes: A Ridiculous-Fishing-style loop: cast, steer the hook down past jellyfish, then hook fish on the way back up, with a hold-to-reel tension minigame for big fish. You sell the catch to upgrade line, hook, lure and boat across 4 waters and 36 species. The art is nice and the loop is solid, but the opening is shallow and slow.

problems: Uneven difficulty between input styles. A fast touch bot got 3 stars on day 1 (919/360) but only 1 star on day 2 (615/510), and a simple zigzag swiper failed day 2 on the phone (397/510). With Playwright mouse input my bots failed day 1 three times (175-229/360). That is partly a test-harness artifact, but day 2 is a sharp wall for a casual swiper.
There is still a lot of the same soil-square grid. The new pond, hay, rocks, trees, sliding rows, tractors and sprinklers break it up, but the core view is the same field screen every day.
The upgrade shop is plain cards with dot bars and only 7 lines. That's fine, but it adds little excitement.
farm-loop.notes: Remade 2026-11-19 (was 2). Fruit-Ninja-style swipe harvester. The fixes landed: the field changes each day (5x3 start, ponds, hay and rocks that break combos, trees, sliding rows), tractor and sprinkler power-ups, chickens that scatter, customers on a market path, tougher stars (1.6x and 2.3x the goal) and bosses. The phone 🏆 is fixed (opens and stays open).

problems: The first league is far beyond a kid. Rookie Row rivals type 36/40/43 WPM, and the first passage has quotes, '#12', '--' and '3/8"'. My 23 WPM 'kid' run placed 4th (last) and only got 'TOP 2 NEEDED'. There's no easy first win, which breaks Rule 1.

The race view is flat: four horizontal dashed lanes with small static car sprites sliding right over a dark band, and the cars have no animation, boost, drafting or reaction to your streaks. The big text box is what you stare at the whole time, so it reads like a typing test with a progress bar.

Progression is the same race repeated: place top 2 twice to move up a league with rivals +10 WPM, 11 times over. Results are a keyboard error heatmap and stats, which are useful but not exciting. There are no streak powers, combo meter or surprise events during the race.
ghost-typer.notes: A typing race: each correct key moves your car along a lane against 3 AI rivals and ghost replays of your best and last runs. You place top 2 twice to climb 11 leagues from 40 to 140 WPM, with an error heatmap and online racing. It's solid for adult typists, but harsh and visually flat for a kid.

problems: Castle 1 (levels 1-10) uses only gems, holes and the gate. The first new idea (rook guards) arrives at level 11, so the first ~10 minutes feel identical. Levels 1-5 are 3-7 forced hops and each one took me 3-7 seconds to clear.

The board is a flat, static checkerboard. Guards never move, tiles have no life, and a hop is a small arc plus a gem pop, with no squash or landing dust. Screen shake fires only on captures and deaths. The castle theme lives on the title screen and barely reaches play.

Nothing surprises you: no secrets, critters, rare events or funny fails. The results panel ('Perfect! 3 stars, Next') has no count-up and no tease of the next level. Tutorial bug: if you keep hopping during 'Undo takes a hop back' and reach the gate, Undo is blocked (the level counts as won), so the tutorial stalls until you press Skip.
knight-quest.notes: Turn-based chess-knight puzzle: tap a glowing square to L-hop, collect every gem, exit through the gate. Later castles add rooks/bishops, walls, crumbling tiles, keys and teleports. Controls are clean (tap, or arrows+Enter, plus undo/hint), but play is a slow, quiet logic puzzle.

problems: The puzzles are shallow. Par is 1-10 moves and early levels need 1-5 taps or drags, so my scripted solver cleared each level in 2-5 seconds and the full set of 45 takes about 30 minutes. Each lab of 9 levels reuses one piece set (mirrors, then splitters, then filters, then prisms), so levels 2-9 of a lab feel like level 1 again.

Weak juice: rotating a mirror is an instant flip, and powering a target gives a small particle burst, then a 'Powered up' panel. No beam charge-up, no rising pitch as targets chain, no slow-mo or full-screen payoff, and the only animation is the beam's slow-moving dashes.

The look is generic glowing neon lines on a navy grid of identical rounded squares, which is exactly the 'random neon / AI look' Charlie rejects. There is no lab world, no characters and nothing reacting to the lasers, and nothing unexpected ever happens.
laser-lab.notes: REMAKE PENDING: a remake scored 7 (needs 8) and was NOT shipped; it is saved on branch wip-tuneup-2026-11-19. Next week: finish it from that branch with these fixes: From level 4 on, drop the preview to 1 bounce (0 on trick-shot levels) and redesign levels to need 2-3 ordered bank shots (shielded and armoured goo, moving blockers), aiming for 20-60 s per level.; Make the arena itself react: flasks that shatter, vents that puff, mirrors that glow, goo that splats onto walls. Swap the checkerboard for a floor that fits each lab.; Lower the star gates (for example 25 / 45 / 65) or count each level's first clear as 2 stars, so clearing every level always opens the next lab.; Update the build/meta.json blurb, for example 'Aim, bounce your laser off walls and mirrors, and zap all the goo!'.. Original: Static grid puzzle: tap mirrors and splitters to flip them, and drag pieces from a tray to route coloured beams into matching receivers, with move-count stars. It works fine on mouse and touch but plays like a quiet worksheet.

problems: Only the numbers change between levels. All 40 levels are the same timed Boggle board: time drops from 100s to 75s, the target rises from 60 to 1030, the grid grows to 6x6 at level 16 and 4-letter words become required at level 23. Level 40 plays like level 1 with a bigger target.

The difficulty curve is broken. Level 1's 3-star score is 96, which a good player passes about 24 times over (my solver scored 2307 there). Late targets, like 1030 points in 75 seconds with 4-letter minimum words on boards full of Qu, J and X, are out of reach for a 9-year-old who finds 3-4 letter words worth about 5-12 points each.

The dictionary accepts obscure and kid-unsuitable words (GESTAPO, DIKTAT, HIEMAL, INHERED, GENEVAS show up in results). The 'Smash' tiles are rare: bombs spawn on about 3.5% of new tiles, so smashing almost never happens and play stays plain word-spotting.
letter-lattice.notes: Boggle-style word swipe against a timer. Drag through adjacent letter tiles (or type them), score pops up with a combo multiplier, tiles drop in, and 2L/gold/bomb/clock specials unlock over the first levels. The swipe feels good, but every level is the same board chasing a bigger number.

problems: The economy is both too slow and too shallow. My first trips earned $60-240, and refuel plus repair ate $40-70 of that each time, while upgrades start at $150, so early runs feel pointless. Yet there are only 6 upgrades x 5 tiers ($73.8k total), and the 5000+ cash core bonus can buy most of them. That breaks Rule 11's 10+ tiers and hours of progression.

Core play is monotonous. Drilling takes about 0.3-0.5 seconds per tile, and you hold Down through a straight shaft for minutes, inside a small light circle that hides ore. You can't plan routes, and moment to moment, 50m feels the same as 150m. The deeper layers do change colour and add lava, gas, crystals and boulders.

There are no safety cues. The shop lets you leave with low hull and no warning, and my pod died from fall damage seconds after leaving. On the 1280-wide title screen the dirt world stops and the right side is a black void. On phone the 4-way d-pad plus two action buttons cover the bottom third of the screen.
mine-deep.notes: Motherload-style drill pod: drive off the pad, hold arrows to dig down through 6 layers, grab ore, fly back to sell, buy drill/tank/cargo/hull/radar/bomb upgrades, and aim for the core at 1000m. It has the most pull of the five, but it's slow to start and samey within a dive.

problems: The first holes don't hook. Hole 1 is an empty straight lane to the cup, and holes 2-6 add one static bumper, sand, slope or water patch each, with few moving set pieces until the Frost and Neon courses. Most holes are one or two putts and done, and a good aim gets lots of holes-in-one (my solver aced 3 of the first 5).

The feel is thin. A tiny white ball rolls with a faint trail across flat vector shapes. There's no squash, no screen shake on wall hits, no slow-mo on a near-miss lip-out, and no characters or reactive world. The cup is a burst plus a 'HOLE IN ONE!' card. The Neon course is again a plain purple grid with a pink border.

It's short, with little to come back for: 27 holes (about 25 minutes for all of them), and the only long-term pull is ball skins. Visual bug: on hole 1 the tutorial spotlight draws a green/orange diagonal beam from the screen's top-left corner to the ball, on both desktop and phone.
pocket-golf.notes: Top-down minigolf: drag back from the ball and release (or arrows plus Space), with bumpers, sand, slopes, water, ice, spinners and teleporters across 3 nine-hole courses and a scorecard after each hole. It's competent and clear, but flat to look at and quick to finish.

_notes.notes: Firebase not set up yet, so plays = null. All games were under 14 days old this run; the never-fun-passed 2026-11-08 batch (11 days old) was treated as eligible.
